title: Frog — Habit, Habitat and External Features
topicTitle: Frog (Rana tigrina): Habit and habitat, external features
notes: **Habit and habitat:** amphibious, lives in water and on land. Found near ponds, lakes, streams. Nocturnal, feeds on insects.

**Body division:** head (no neck, eyes with nictitating membrane, tympanum for hearing), trunk (no tail in adult, short forelimbs with 4 fingers, long hindlimbs with 5 webbed toes for swimming), cloaca (common exit for digestive, urinary and reproductive tracts).
**Skin:** moist, glandular, mucus-secreting for cutaneous respiration. Pigmented for camouflage. Mucous glands keep skin moist; poison glands in some species.
**Skeletal adaptations:** vertebral column short and rigid. Skull flattened. Hind-limbs elongated with fused bones (tibiofibula) for jumping. Urostyle supports hind-limbs.
**Digestive system:** alimentary canal short because carnivorous diet. Tongue bifid at tip, attached at front, free at back, thrown out to catch prey.

**Eyes:** large and prominent, located dorsolaterally on the head giving wide field of vision for detecting prey and predators. Upper eyelid is fixed; lower eyelid is movable. A transparent third eyelid called the nictitating membrane covers the eye during swimming or on land to keep it moist and protected from debris.

**Tympanum (ear drum):** large circular membrane visible behind each eye. It detects sound vibrations in both air and water. Males often have a larger tympanum than females, which helps in detecting calls during breeding season.

**Colour and camouflage:** dorsal surface is olive-green or brown with dark spots for blending with muddy and vegetated surroundings. Ventral surface is pale or yellowish-white. Some species exhibit countershading — dark on top and light below — to reduce visibility from predators above and below.

**Locomotion adaptations:** forelimbs are short with four unwebbed fingers used for propping the body during rest and landing after jumps. Hind-limbs are much longer and powerful with five webbed toes; the webbing acts as a paddle for swimming. The elongated tarsal bones (astragalus and calcaneum) provide leverage for jumping distances up to 10–20 times body length.

**Skin glands and secretion:** two types of glands — mucous glands (keep skin moist, aid cutaneous respiration) and poison or granular glands (secrete toxic or distasteful substances for defense against predators). The poison glands are concentrated on the dorsal surface and behind the tympanum in many species.

**Adaptation to dual life:** frog can respire through skin, buccal lining, and lungs — an adaptation for transitioning between aquatic and terrestrial environments. Webbed feet aid swimming; powerful hind-limbs aid jumping on land. Moist skin is a limitation — frog must stay near water sources to prevent desiccation.

**Nocturnal behaviour:** frog is primarily active at night (nocturnal) when humidity is higher, reducing water loss through skin. During the day it hides under rocks, vegetation, or burrows into mud. This behaviour also helps avoid diurnal predators.

**Diet and feeding:** frog is carnivorous in adult stage. It feeds on insects, worms, snails, and small invertebrates. The sticky bifid tongue is projected rapidly to capture prey. Teeth (vomerine and maxillary) are present only in the upper jaw and help in holding prey but not in chewing.

**Mouth and buccal cavity:** the mouth opens into a large buccal cavity. In males, a pair of vocal sacs (inflation chambers) are present at the angles of the lower jaw. These sacs amplify the croaking sound during breeding season to attract females.

**Nictitating membrane function — the translucent third eyelid moves horizontally across the eye, protecting it from debris and desiccation while still allowing the frog to see. This is crucial when the frog is on land, as it prevents the eye from drying out while maintaining visual acuity for detecting predators and prey.

**Tympanic membrane acoustics — the tympanic membrane (tympanum) is tensed by the muscle tensor tympani and connected to the inner ear via the columellar bone (stapes homologue). In aquatic environments, vibrations travel efficiently through the membrane to the inner ear, while in air, the membrane acts as a pressure receiver, transmitting sound waves to the cochlea for directional hearing during mate attraction.

**Urostyle skeletal adaptation — the urostyle (urostylian process) is a bony rod formed by the fusion of anterior caudal vertebrae to the sacrum. This structure provides a rigid anchor for the powerful hind-limb muscles (quadriceps and gastrocnemius), enabling the explosive jumping mechanism that propels the frog up to 20 times its body length in a single bound.

**Countercurrent heat exchange in limbs — the arteries supplying the hind-limb muscles pass closely alongside the veins returning from the feet, creating a countercurrent heat exchanger. This conserves core body temperature during cold nights and prevents overheating during midday basking, allowing the frog to maintain optimal enzymatic activity despite fluctuating environmental temperatures.

**Cutaneous glandular distribution — the granular glands (poison glands) are innervated by sympathetic nerve fibers, so their secretion is triggered by stress or predation attempts. Alkaloid compounds like bufotoxins are released, deterring predators such as snakes and birds. The mucous glands, by contrast, are under parasympathetic control and continuously secrete a watery mucus rich in glycoproteins and lysozyme to prevent pathogen colonisation.

**Sexual dimorphism in external features — adult male frogs possess nuptial pads (keratinised, rough-textured skin) on the first finger and forelimbs, used for gripping the female during amplexus. Males also tend to be smaller than females and produce advertisement calls. Females lack nuptial pads and typically have a larger, more rounded body to accommodate egg production.

**Thermoregulatory behavioural adaptations — frogs are ectothermic and regulate body temperature through behavioural means: basking in sunny spots with limbs extended to maximise heat absorption, seeking shade or burrowing during peak heat, and orienting the body to present the minimum or maximum surface area to the sun or wind as needed. The dark dorsal colouration also enhances solar heat absorption.

**Frogcroak vocal apparatus — during calling, the male closes its glottis, contracts the vocal sac muscles, and forces air from the lungs past the vocal cords (folded in the larynx), producing the characteristic croak. The vocal sac inflates like a resonator, amplifying the sound. Different species produce distinct call patterns (frequency, duration, pulse rate) that are species-specific and crucial for mate recognition.
confusion: Frog has moist skin and lives in water — it is NOT a fish. Frog is an amphibian because it can live on both land and water, has lungs for air-breathing as an adult, and undergoes metamorphosis from a fish-like tadpole.

Frog has a three-chambered heart (two auricles, one ventricle) — do NOT confuse with fish (two-chambered) or reptiles/birds/mammals (four-chambered). The single ventricle causes some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Webbed toes are for swimming, NOT for walking. The webbing is a thin skin membrane between the toes that increases surface area for pushing water, similar to a paddle.

The tympanum is NOT an ear pinna (outer ear) like in humans. It is a flat, circular membrane on the surface of the skin that directly transmits vibrations to the inner ear without an external ear canal.

Nictitating membrane is NOT the same as the eyelid. It is a translucent third eyelid that partially covers the eye for protection while still allowing partial vision, unlike the opaque upper and lower eyelids.

Mistaking the cloaca for a single organ — Correct explanation: the cloaca is not a true organ but a common chamber formed by the convergence of the terminal parts of the digestive, urinary, and reproductive tracts. It serves as the single opening for all three systems, and its walls contain fold-like structures (cloacal bursae) that can aid in sperm storage during mating.

Confusing mucous glands with poison glands — Correct explanation: mucous glands are smaller, tubular, and distributed throughout the skin; they secrete a watery mucus to keep the skin moist for respiration and protection. Poison (granular) glands are larger, more concentrated, and produce toxic secretions for defence. They are histologically distinct and serve opposite primary functions.

Thinking all frogs have identical external colouration — Correct explanation: while Rana tigrina is typically olive-green with dark spots, other frog species exhibit wildly different patterns, including bright warning colours (aposematic), cryptic leaf-mimicry patterns, or even translucent skin. Colouration is highly species-specific and tied to habitat, predator pressure, and thermoregulatory needs.

Assuming the tongue is attached at the back like in mammals — Correct explanation: in frogs, the tongue is attached at the FRONT of the lower jaw (anteriorly), not the back. This forward attachment allows the tongue to be projected forward and backward with great speed and force to capture prey, whereas a rearward attachment would limit projection ability.

Misconceiving nuptial pads as permanent structures — Correct explanation: nuptial pads develop only during the breeding season under the influence of testosterone. Outside the breeding season, they regress. They are formed by hyperplasia of the epidermis and dermal papillae, creating a rough surface for grip. This seasonal development links them directly to reproductive activity, not general locomotion.

Believing frogs drown if submerged — Correct explanation: frogs can absorb oxygen through their highly vascularised skin and the lining of the mouth and cloaca even while submerged. They do not drown but rely entirely on cutaneous respiration underwater. Lungs are only needed in air, and some species remain aquatic their entire lives without ever using lungs.

Describe how the external features of a frog (tympanum, eyes, skin colour) help it survive in its natural pond habitat.
A student claims that a frog can breathe only through its lungs. Identify the error and list all three respiratory surfaces a frog uses.
How does the webbed foot of a frog function differently from the hoof of a horse? Explain in terms of habitat adaptation.

A herpetologist observes that male frogs in a population have significantly larger tympanums than females. Formulate a hypothesis to explain this observation and design a simple experiment to test whether the tympanum size affects mating success.

Predict and compare the activity levels, skin condition, and survival time for each group, providing physiological reasons for your predictions.

Explain how the distribution pattern of mucous and poison glands in frog skin reflects an evolutionary trade-off between respiration and defence. Include the roles of the autonomic nervous system in regulating each gland type.
universalFacts: Rana tigrina (Indian bullfrog) is the most commonly studied frog species in Indian school biology curricula and is widely distributed across the Indian subcontinent.
A frog can absorb water directly through its skin (pelvic patch) — it does not need to drink water through its mouth like mammals do.
The nictitating membrane is a shared feature with many reptiles and birds, showing an evolutionary link between these groups and amphibians.
Frog skin must remain moist for cutaneous respiration; mucus secretion can increase up to 50 times when the frog is stressed or in dry conditions.
The tongue of a frog can be projected out of the mouth in about 0.07 seconds, making it one of the fastest feeding mechanisms among vertebrates.

Anurans (frogs and toads) are the only vertebrates with a urostyle — a fused set of caudal vertebrae that forms a rigid rod supporting the pelvis and hind-limbs, having lost the tail during evolution.

The columellar bone in the frog's middle ear is homologous to the stapes in mammals, both derived from the same embryonic hyoid arch, demonstrating a shared evolutionary origin of hearing structures across tetrapods.
Frog skin contains approximately 2,000–3,000 granular glands per square centimetre, making it one of the most densely gland-populated epithelial surfaces among vertebrates.
The eyes of a frog occupy about 1/3 of the skull volume, giving them exceptional visual acuity for detecting both prey and predators at distances up to 3–5 metres in daylight conditions.

Nuptial pads in male frogs contain up to 15 times more keratin than the surrounding skin, creating a sandpaper-like texture that prevents slippage during the male's grip on the female's slippery skin during amplexus.

The frog's tympanic membrane can detect sound frequencies ranging from 100 Hz to 2,500 Hz, with peak sensitivity around 600–800 Hz — the range of conspecific advertisement calls, making it exquisitely tuned for mate recognition.
